passage: On Wednesday the fest committee chalked out the stalls in the school hall. Minakshi, who was running the lemonade and snacks stall, sat on the steps with Vasudha and a notebook. 'Imagine it's Saturday night and the stall flopped,' she said. 'Why?' She wrote as they talked: not enough change ready, so people walk off; rain, and the stall is in the open courtyard; a poor spot behind the science block. Vasudha added, 'And the sugar might run out by noon.' Minakshi hadn't thought of any of that when she had only planned how many people would come. Beside each item she wrote a small fix: coins from the shop counter at home, a tarp from the caretaker, asking the committee to swap the spot, and double the sugar.

qa.q: Which reasons for a flop did Minakshi write herself?
qa.a: Minakshi wrote not enough change ready, rain in the open courtyard, and a poor spot behind the science block.

qa.q: What does the notebook suggest about how Minakshi now feels about the stall?
qa.a: Minakshi seems more prepared and realistic, having seen that her first plan was too hopeful.

qa.q: What other approach could Minakshi use to find more risks?
qa.a: Minakshi could ask a teacher or senior who ran a stall last year what went wrong for them, since they may know problems she has not met.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have seen the exercise?
qa.a: Vasudha probably felt useful, since adding the sugar risk showed that two people spot more than one.

grounding: Shows a teenager imagining that the fest stall flopped and writing down reasons in advance, which surfaces risks that hopeful planning skipped.

passage:
Dear Kunal,
I know you think I'm being gloomy, but hear me out before Friday's fest.
Last night I tried something. I pretended it was Saturday and our bookmark stall had completely flopped. Then I asked myself: why did it flop? I wrote down whatever came.
1. People paid with big notes and we had no change, so they walked off.
2. It rained, and paper bookmarks got soggy.
3. We got the corner behind the stage where nobody walks.
None of these were in our plan. Our plan was only colours and prices!
So can you bring a bag of ten-rupee notes and coins from your dad's shop? I'll get plastic sleeves and a tarp. And let's ask Mrs Pillai tomorrow if we can swap for a spot near the food stalls.
Not gloomy. Just ready.
Keerthana

qa.q: What did Keerthana plan to get to protect against rain?
qa.a: Keerthana planned to get plastic sleeves and a tarp.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt after writing down the three reasons?
qa.a: Keerthana probably felt uneasy at first and then more confident and ready, since the list showed gaps the colourful plan had missed.

qa.q: What else could Keerthana and Kunal do to test the stall before Friday?
qa.a: They could do a short trial run at home, pretending to sell to family, to catch any other problems like slow counting or missing price tags.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the letter?
qa.a: Kunal might first think Keerthana is being gloomy, then feel reassured, because each worry now comes with a clear job for each of them.

grounding: It shows a teenager imagining the fest stall has already failed, listing change, rain and location as reasons, and finding risks the hopeful plan skipped.

passage:
So, Jagdish, you want to know why our ring-toss stall made the most money at the fest? It's because of one weird evening, the Wednesday before.
Your friend Arnab was sitting on the terrace feeling great about the plan. Rings, bottles, prizes, done. Then I thought, okay, imagine it's over and it was a disaster. Why?
First thing that came: nobody has change. Everyone brings a hundred, tickets are ten. Second: what if it rains, the bottles are on the open ground. Third: they'd put us near the toilets last year.
I actually laughed, because all three were so obvious and none were on my list.
So I got two hundred in coins from the vegetable vendor, borrowed a big umbrella from the canteen, and went to the fest committee on Thursday to ask for a spot by the main gate.
It drizzled at noon. We didn't even notice.

qa.q: What did Arnab borrow from the canteen?
qa.a: Arnab borrowed a big umbrella from the canteen.

qa.q: Why did Arnab laugh while listing the reasons for a disaster?
qa.a: Arnab felt surprised and a bit embarrassed that all three risks were so obvious yet missing from the list.

qa.q: What else could Arnab try in next year's planning, and why?
qa.a: Arnab could ask a friend to do the same imagined-failure exercise separately, since another person may spot risks Arnab overlooks.

qa.q: How might the fest committee see Arnab's request on Thursday?
qa.a: They may see a student who has thought ahead, which can make them more willing to give a better spot by the main gate.

grounding: It shows a teenager imagining the fest stall has flopped, naming no change, rain and poor location, and so catching risks the cheerful plan missed.
